summary: This document specifies a general channel mechanism, as extensions to TRILL, for sending messages such as BFD between RBridges and between RBridges and end stations in an RBridge campus.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7178 defines a general way for TRILL switches, called RBridges, to exchange messages beyond ordinary TRILL data and routing messages. A shared channel format can carry protocols such as BFD between RBridges and, in a native form, between an RBridge and a directly connected end station.

how does trill carry bfd messages
subtitle: A shared TRILL channel format for messages between RBridges and directly connected end stations.

tldr.problem: The TRILL base protocol carried TRILL data and IS-IS messages but did not define a general way to carry other control protocols such as Bidirectional Forwarding Detection.
tldr.mechanism: An RBridge Channel message uses a special inner destination MAC address and Ethertype, followed by a channel header that identifies the protocol. It can travel as a TRILL Data frame or as a native frame on a directly connected link.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can share one channel format for unicast, multi-hop and multi-destination messages. RFC 7178 is updated by RFC 7978.

today: RFC 7178 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014 and is updated by RFC 7978. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why TRILL Has a Channel
sections.content:
TRILL devices are called Routing Bridges (RBridges). The base TRILL protocol defines TRILL Data messages and TRILL IS-IS messages, but protocols such as BFD need another way to exchange messages at the TRILL layer.

This RFC defines one general RBridge Channel mechanism instead of a separate carriage method for each protocol. It supports one-hop and multi-hop unicast as well as VLAN-scoped multi-destination delivery. It also defines a native format for communication with end stations directly attached to an RBridge.
sections.plainLanguage: RBridges need a standard way to carry control messages that are not ordinary TRILL data. The channel gives those protocols a shared message format.

sections.title: The Inter-RBridge Frame
sections.content:
Between RBridges, a channel message is carried in a TRILL Data frame. The inner destination is the All-Egress-RBridges multicast address, and the inner Ethertype identifies an RBridge Channel message. The frame contains the link header, TRILL header, inner Ethernet header, channel header, protocol-specific data and link trailer.

The channel header starts with the RBridge-Channel Ethertype and has a 4-bit header version, a 12-bit Channel Protocol, 12 flag bits and a 4-bit error field. This document specifies header version zero and protocol value 0x001 for RBridge Channel Error. The Silent, Multi-Hop and Native flags are defined; reserved flag bits are sent as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame carries an inner channel header that identifies the protocol and marks message properties. The remaining payload belongs to that protocol.

sections.title: TRILL Delivery, Nicknames and VLANs
sections.content:
The TRILL header identifies ingress and egress RBridges and whether a message is unicast or multi-destination. A newly originated message uses the maximum Hop Count, 0x3F, unless its channel protocol specifies another value. The Any-RBridge nickname lets a one-hop unicast reach an immediate neighbor regardless of nickname state.

The inner VLAN tag is present. Multi-destination messages are scoped to the VLAN of interest. Known-unicast messages use VLAN 1 by default. The RFC recommends priority 7 for one-hop messages critical to connectivity, priority 6 for other important unicast messages, and the default priority of zero for other messages; priorities above 5 should not be used for that last category.
sections.plainLanguage: The TRILL header names the source and destination RBridges and controls how far the message travels. VLAN and priority fields keep delivery within the intended network scope.

sections.title: Processing Messages and Reporting Errors
sections.content:
RBridges normally forward channel frames as TRILL Data frames. An RBridge Channel Alert flag can request processing by transit RBridges. At egress, an RBridge checks the channel header and protocol. It discards malformed frames, including those with an unsupported header version, an unknown protocol or an invalid Native flag.

When appropriate, an RBridge Channel Error message reports the problem to the originator and includes the first 256 bytes of the erroneous message, or fewer if fewer are available. The Silent flag, rate limiting and other conditions can suppress an error. An RBridge must not generate an error in response to another error message.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiving RBridge checks whether it can process the channel frame. It may send a limited error report, but it must not create an endless chain of error replies.

sections.title: Native Frames and Protocol Support
sections.content:
A channel protocol may use native RBridge Channel frames between an RBridge and an end station on the same link. These frames have the RBridge-Channel Ethertype and channel header but no TRILL header. The Native flag must be set. A VLAN tag is not required by TRILL, though the link or protocol may require one.

RBridges advertise supported channel protocols through TLVs or sub-TLVs in their Link State PDUs. Channel messages should normally be sent only to RBridges that advertise support for the protocol. Protocol number 1, the error protocol, must be supported by any RBridge that implements the channel facility.
sections.plainLanguage: Some protocols can use the same channel format directly on a local link, without a TRILL header. RBridges advertise which channel protocols they support.

sections.title: Congestion, Allocations and Security
sections.content:
Channel traffic should be small relative to link capacity. Outgoing messages should be rate limited, especially when they are high priority, multi-destination or multi-hop. Connectivity-checking protocols such as BFD should use less than 5% of the associated link bitrate. Incoming messages may also be rate limited to reduce denial-of-service risk.

IANA assigned the Any-RBridge nickname 0xFFC0, the multicast addresses TRILL-End-Stations and All-Edge-RBridges, and registries for channel protocols, flags and errors. The IEEE Registration Authority assigned Ethertype 0x8946. The channel itself provides no general authentication, integrity or encryption; a protocol that needs those services must provide them.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel messages must not consume too much link capacity. The channel does not secure messages by itself, so each protocol must supply any authentication or privacy protection it needs.

viz.caption: LAYERS IN AN INTER-RBRIDGE CHANNEL FRAME

layers.label: Link header
layers.detail: Carries the frame to the next-hop RBridge.

layers.label: TRILL header
layers.detail: Carries ingress and egress nicknames and Hop Count.

layers.label: Inner Ethernet header
layers.detail: Contains the All-Egress-RBridges destination and VLAN.

layers.label: RBridge Channel header
layers.detail: Identifies channel protocol, flags and error field.

layers.label: Link trailer
layers.detail: Includes the Ethernet FCS on Ethernet links.
